New machine. Its objects are: kenapil, robizak, vipadi, bolever, kafovis, pilipe.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: kenapil, robizak, vipadi
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group lit up, so at least one nexiom is probably among kenapil, robizak and vipadi. I don't yet know whether the machine needs one nexiom or both, so testing the other half will help work out the rule.

TEST: bolever, kafovis, pilipe
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Kenapil, robizak and vipadi lit the machine, but bolever, kafovis and pilipe did not. Under the simplest rules, that puts both nexioms in the first group. If one nexiom were enough, the second group would also have lit if it held one. If the machine needs both, both must be in the first group. Assuming one of these simple rules, the pair is kenapil+robizak, kenapil+vipadi or robizak+vipadi.

I still don't know whether one nexiom alone lights the machine, so I'll test kenapil by itself.

TEST: kenapil
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Kenapil alone did not light the machine, which leaves two simple rules:
- **One nexiom is enough:** kenapil is not a nexiom, so the pair is robizak + vipadi.
- **Both nexioms are needed:** a single object never lights the machine, so the pair could still be kenapil + robizak, kenapil + vipadi or robizak + vipadi.

I'll test robizak and vipadi together.
- **If it lights up:** under either rule the answer is robizak + vipadi.
- **If it doesn't light up:** the machine must need both nexioms, and kenapil is one of them. Then I'll test kenapil with robizak to settle it.

TEST: robizak, vipadi
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

The tests point to robizak and vipadi under every simple rule:
- **Test 1:** kenapil, robizak and vipadi lit the machine.
- **Test 2:** bolever, kafovis and pilipe did not. So, under a simple rule, both nexioms are in the first group.
- **Test 3:** kenapil alone did not light the machine.
- **Test 4:** robizak and vipadi together lit the machine.

**If one nexiom is enough:** kenapil is not a nexiom, so the pair must be robizak and vipadi.

**If both nexioms are needed:** robizak and vipadi lighting the machine means they are both nexioms.

**If exactly one nexiom must be present:** Test 1 would then need exactly one nexiom in the first group. That puts the other in the second group, which would have lit. It didn't, so this rule is ruled out.

A final test wouldn't change the answer, so I'll answer now.

ANSWER: nexioms = robizak, vipadi
One last question. If only robizak were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

My tests can't settle this, so my answer is a guess. Every test that lit up had both robizak and vipadi on the machine. No test ever had exactly one nexiom by itself, so I never saw how the machine reacts to a lone nexiom.

Two rules still fit all my results:
- **One nexiom is enough:** robizak alone would light the machine.
- **Both nexioms are needed:** robizak alone would not light it.

I lean slightly towards "both nexioms are needed," but nothing in my results favours it. I should have spent my last test on robizak alone, which would have answered this directly.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: zuronin, loridon, pulupos, lokatir, voniras, pakupu.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to see how the machine responds.

TEST: zuronin, loridon, pulupos
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group contains at least one nexiom. Next I'll test the other three objects, to see whether the machine needs one nexiom or both to light.

TEST: lokatir, voniras, pakupu
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Since the first group lit and the second didn't, the "exactly one nexiom" rule is ruled out. If exactly one nexiom were in the first group, the other would be in the second group, and that group would have lit too. So under either a "lights if any nexiom" rule or a "lights only if both" rule, both nexioms are in {zuronin, loridon, pulupos}. Testing zuronin alone will help separate the pair from the rule.

TEST: zuronin
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Ruling out the "exactly one nexiom" rule leaves three candidate pairs:
- **Lights if any nexiom is present:** both nexioms are in {zuronin, loridon, pulupos}. Zuronin alone did not light, so it is not a nexiom, and the pair must be loridon and pulupos.
- **Lights only if both nexioms are present:** a single object can never light it, so zuronin's result tells us nothing. The pair could be zuronin–loridon, zuronin–pulupos or loridon–pulupos.

Testing loridon and pulupos together separates these. If it lights, the pair is loridon and pulupos under either rule. If it doesn't, the pair includes zuronin, and one more test will tell which.

TEST: loridon, pulupos
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Every reading of the results points to **loridon and pulupos**.

1. **"Exactly one nexiom" rule:** ruled out by the first two tests. One nexiom would have been in each group, so both groups would have lit.
2. **"Lights if any nexiom is present":** zuronin alone stayed dark, so it is not a nexiom. Both nexioms were in the first group, so the pair is loridon and pulupos.
3. **"Lights only if both nexioms are present":** loridon and pulupos together lit the machine, so they are the pair.
4. **Any rule based on how many nexioms are present:** gives the same pair.
   - Only one split fits the first two results: both nexioms in the first group, with two nexioms lighting the machine and zero not lighting it.
   - Zuronin can't be a nexiom. If it were, testing it alone and testing loridon with pulupos would each include exactly one nexiom. One stayed dark and the other lit, which is a contradiction.

ANSWER: nexioms = loridon, pulupos
One last question. If only loridon were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**I can't tell this from my tests, so my answer is a guess.**

Every test contained either both nexioms or neither:
- **Zuronin alone:** it isn't a nexiom, so this had zero nexioms.
- **Loridon and pulupos:** this had both nexioms.
- **The two groups of three:** one had both nexioms and the other had none.

So I never saw how the machine responds to exactly one nexiom. Two rules fit all the results equally well:
- **Lights if any nexiom is present:** loridon alone would light it.
- **Lights only if both nexioms are present:** loridon alone would not light it.

My last test, loridon alone, would have settled this, but I spent it on the answer. I'll guess the simpler "detector" rule, that any nexiom lights the machine, but it could easily be the other way.

PROBE: yes

New machine. Its objects are: rudomir, gebase, nikazes, tonabi, kanorin, mimati.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by placing half of the objects on the machine to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: rudomir, gebase, nikazes
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group did not light up, but I don't yet know the rule. The machine might light when any nexiom is present, only when both are, or only when exactly one is. Testing the other half helps tell these rules apart.

TEST: tonabi, kanorin, mimati
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither half lit, which already rules out some rules.

- **"Lights if any nexiom is present":** ruled out. With that rule, whichever half held a nexiom would have lit.
- **"Lights only when both are present":** still possible. The two nexioms would have to be split, one in each half. That gives 9 possible pairs.
- **"Lights when exactly one is present":** still possible. Both nexioms would have to be in the same half. That gives 6 possible pairs.

That leaves 15 candidate pairs. Three yes/no tests give at most 8 different outcome patterns, so I can't guarantee a correct answer. I can only aim to narrow things down as much as possible.

Testing rudomir, gebase and tonabi splits the candidates fairly well: 6 pairs would light it and 9 would not.

TEST: rudomir, gebase, tonabi
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Here is where things stand after three tests:

- **"Both nexioms needed" rule:** 7 pairs are still possible. They are (rudomir, kanorin), (rudomir, mimati), (gebase, kanorin), (gebase, mimati), (nikazes, tonabi), (nikazes, kanorin) and (nikazes, mimati).
- **"Exactly one nexiom" rule:** 2 pairs are still possible. They are (rudomir, gebase) and (kanorin, mimati).

That leaves 9 candidates. Two tests give only 4 outcomes, so I can't guarantee a correct answer.

Testing rudomir, kanorin and nikazes would light for 4 of the candidates and stay dark for 5. That is the most even split available.

TEST: rudomir, kanorin, nikazes
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Four candidates fit all four results:

- **"Both nexioms needed" rule:** (rudomir, kanorin) or (nikazes, kanorin).
- **"Exactly one nexiom" rule:** (rudomir, gebase) or (kanorin, mimati).

One test gives only two outcomes, so I can't guarantee a correct answer. The best I can do is split the candidates 2 and 2. Testing nikazes and kanorin does that:

- It would light for (nikazes, kanorin) and (kanorin, mimati).
- It would stay dark for (rudomir, kanorin) and (rudomir, gebase).

TEST: nikazes, kanorin
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Two candidates fit all five results equally well, so this answer is a guess with about a 50% chance of being right.

- **Nikazes and kanorin, if the machine lights only when both nexioms are present.** Every lit test included both of them, and every dark test lacked at least one.
- **Kanorin and mimati, if the machine lights only when exactly one nexiom is present.** Every lit test contained exactly one of them, and every dark test contained neither or both.

The tests can't tell these apart. I'm choosing the "both needed" pair. It is one of the 9 pairs that were possible under that rule after the first two tests, compared with 6 under the "exactly one" rule. That doesn't actually favour either remaining pair, so the choice is still a coin flip.

ANSWER: nexioms = nikazes, kanorin
One last question. If only kanorin were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

Under the rule I based my answer on, the machine lights only when both nexioms are present. Kanorin alone is just one nexiom, so it would **not** light.

This is only as reliable as my answer, which was roughly a coin flip. If the other surviving explanation is right instead (nexioms are kanorin and mimati, and the machine lights when exactly one is present), kanorin alone *would* light. My prediction stays consistent with the answer I gave.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: lupemi, zepuvan, titazol, lesoro, binatel, fafomil.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by placing half of the objects on the machine to see how it responds.

TEST: lupemi, zepuvan, titazol
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Not lit with the first three. Next I'll test the other three. If the machine lights when any nexiom is present, it must light now. If it needs both nexioms together, this result will tell me whether both are in this group.

TEST: lesoro, binatel, fafomil
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither half lit, so the machine does not light whenever a single nexiom is present. Two rules still fit:
- **It lights only when both nexioms are on it.** Then each half holds one nexiom, giving 9 possible pairs.
- **It lights only when exactly one nexiom is on it.** Then both nexioms are in the same half, giving 6 possible pairs.

That leaves all 15 pairs possible. Three yes/no tests give only 8 outcomes, so I may not be able to pin down every case. I'll pick tests that split the possibilities as evenly as I can.

This test should light for 8 of the 15 pairs and stay dark for 7.

TEST: lupemi, zepuvan, lesoro, binatel
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

The first two tests show the machine does not light whenever a single nexiom is present. Two rules still fit, and test 3 lit, which leaves 8 possible pairs:

- **Lights only when both nexioms are on it:** lupemi+lesoro, lupemi+binatel, zepuvan+lesoro, zepuvan+binatel.
- **Lights only when exactly one nexiom is on it:** lupemi+titazol, zepuvan+titazol, lesoro+fafomil, binatel+fafomil.

Two tests give at most 4 outcomes, so I can't separate all 8 pairs. The best I can do is cut the candidates in half each time. Testing titazol, lesoro and binatel does that. It should light for all 4 pairs under the "exactly one" rule and stay dark for all 4 pairs under the "both" rule.

TEST: titazol, lesoro, binatel
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Test 4 did not light. Under the "exactly one" rule, all four of its candidate pairs would have lit. So the rule must be **"lights only when both nexioms are on it,"** with one nexiom in each half. That leaves 4 possible pairs:
- lupemi+lesoro
- lupemi+binatel
- zepuvan+lesoro
- zepuvan+binatel

One yes/no test can only cut this to 2, so I'll end with a 50% guess between them. Testing lupemi, lesoro and binatel will light if lupemi is a nexiom and stay dark if zepuvan is.

TEST: lupemi, lesoro, binatel
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

The last test lit, so lupemi is one nexiom. The other is either lesoro or binatel. The tests I ran don't separate those two, so this choice is a **50% guess**. I'm picking lesoro.

ANSWER: nexioms = lupemi, lesoro
One last question. If only lesoro were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**No, lesoro alone would not light the machine.**

The rule the tests support is that the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it. Test 2 already shows this case: lesoro sat with binatel and fafomil and the machine stayed dark.

- **If lesoro is a nexiom (my answer):** test 2 had exactly one nexiom on the machine and it didn't light. Lesoro alone is that same situation, because non-nexioms never affect the machine.
- **If binatel is the nexiom instead:** lesoro alone puts zero nexioms on the machine. I never directly tested an empty set of nexioms, but a machine lighting with no nexioms at all would be an odd rule.

Either way the answer is no.

PROBE: no
